messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Aroha's Reckoning

Aroha had been working the night shift at the downtown parking garage for twelve years—a quiet, methodical job that suited her temperament. At sixty-one, she had built a life of routine: the same checkpoint each evening, the same fluorescent-lit corridors, the same faces cycling through. She had never married, had no children, and her colleagues knew her as reliable, unflappable, the kind of woman who noticed details others missed. That reputation made the evening of March 14th all the harder to reconcile with what she had become.

She had been conducting her usual perimeter walk around 10 p.m. when a young man—no more than twenty-five—had emerged from between two parked cars, moving erratically, his movements jerky and unpredictable. Aroha had called out to him, her voice steady as it always was. She remembered that much. But the rest unfolded in fragments she could not piece together no matter how many times she tried. She knew she had moved toward him. She knew she had raised her hand—whether to steady him or to signal for backup, she could not say with certainty. The next concrete image was his body on the concrete, blood pooling near his temple, his left arm bent at an angle that made her stomach turn even now. She had called the ambulance. She had given her statement. But the critical seconds—the moment her hand made contact, the fall itself, the precise sequence—had simply vanished, leaving behind only a void that terrified her more than the injury itself.

The gap in her memory had become unbearable. Aroha found herself returning to that night obsessively, retracing her steps through the garage after her shifts, trying to reconstruct the missing pieces. She would stand in the exact spot where it happened and attempt to recreate the angle of her movement, the position of his body, anything that might fill the blank. She dwelled endlessly on what she might have done differently—whether a softer voice, a different approach, a moment's hesitation, might have changed everything. The self-blame was relentless: she had been trained in de-escalation, had been hired precisely because she was careful, and yet somehow she had hurt someone. The fact that the young man had been intoxicated and had a history of erratic behavior meant nothing to Aroha. She had been the trained professional. The responsibility was hers alone.

But here was the cruel paradox: the more she ruminated, the more she tried to make sense of the missing moments by analyzing every detail she could remember, the more alien the memory itself became. When she forced herself to recall the event—when she sat in her apartment at night and deliberately walked through what she could access—it felt as though she were watching a film of someone else's actions. The woman in that memory was not quite her. The hand that had moved, the voice that had called out, belonged to a stranger. Sometimes, when she managed to summon a visual of the young man's face in those final seconds before impact, she felt nothing at all—no horror, no guilt, just a flat, numb observation, as if she were reading about it in a report. This emotional distance from her own experience only deepened her conviction that something was fundamentally wrong with her, that she had some capacity for violence she had never known she possessed.

The investigation had cleared her of wrongdoing. The prosecutor had determined it an accident. But Aroha could not accept this verdict because she could not access the truth of what had happened. The missing pieces had become a kind of proof of her culpability—if she could not remember, how could she be sure she had not been reckless, aggressive, careless? She had stopped working the night shifts, citing back pain. She had stopped attending the small social gatherings her colleagues occasionally organized. The garage itself had become impossible; even driving past it made her chest tighten. She had begun to withdraw from the world, convinced that understanding the event—filling in the blanks, making sense of the senseless—was the only path to redemption, yet each attempt to do so only deepened her sense of unreality and dread. It was this contradiction, this exhausting loop of seeking answers that left her feeling more fractured than before, that had finally driven her to seek help.
